name: Smart Contracts and Executable Terms
title: Smart Contracts and Executable Terms
answer: Smart contracts and executable terms refer to contract provisions written so that performance, payment, or other obligations can be triggered automatically by software when defined conditions are met. In the AI lawyer context, this covers drafting clauses that a machine can read and execute, mapping natural language obligations to code, and managing the boundary between legal text and runtime behavior. It also includes reviewing whether an executable term accurately reflects the parties' intent and remains enforceable if the underlying data or oracle fails.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Smart contracts and executable terms refer to contract provisions written so that performance, payment, or other obligations can be triggered automatically by software when defined conditions are met. In the AI lawyer context, this covers drafting clauses that a machine can read and execute, mapping natural language obligations to code, and managing the boundary between legal text and runtime behavior. It also includes reviewing whether an executable term accurately reflects the parties' intent and remains enforceable if the underlying data or oracle fails.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Executable terms run on distributed ledger platforms, private blockchain networks, or centralized workflow engines that can call external data sources known as oracles. The infrastructure includes contract registries, key management systems, and event logs that record when a condition was evaluated and what action followed. Many implementations use a virtual machine that executes bytecode, while simpler systems rely on rule engines or API triggers inside a contract lifecycle management platform.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is done by translating agreed obligations into conditional logic, often with a plain language header that states the legal meaning of each coded term. Drafters and developers work from a term sheet or clause library, then test the code against scenarios such as late payment, missing data, or disputed performance. Reviewers compare the executable code to the natural language clause and check that the trigger conditions, remedies, and fallback paths match the negotiated deal.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk turn on whether the code is the contract or merely evidence of it, and on who controls upgrades, pauses, and dispute resolution. Provenance requires a clear record of which version of a clause was signed, which data source fed the condition, and who had authority to deploy or modify the executable term. Because automated performance can move value without human review, parties typically need access controls, audit trails, and an agreed process for correcting erroneous transfers or oracle failures.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction is toward hybrid contracts that keep natural language as the governing text while using executable terms for routine, low ambiguity steps such as escrow release, royalty payments, or supply chain milestones. Standards for machine readable clauses and formal verification are likely to improve, making it easier to prove that code matches the legal intent before deployment. Courts and regulators are also beginning to address when automated execution creates binding obligations, which will shape how these terms are drafted and enforced.
